title: Cheese and Onion Pasty
subtitle: Sharp cheddar and sweet onion filling in a crimped shortcrust
excerpt: Cheese and onion pasty is the most popular vegetarian pasty in Britain: raw sliced onion, diced potato, and grated strong cheddar sealed inside shortcrust pastry and baked. The onion and potato cook in the steam trapped inside the pastry, and the melted cheese holds the filling together. It is straightforward and very satisfying.
sourceNotes: The cheese and onion pasty is a direct relative of the Cornish pasty, following the same method of sealing raw ingredients into shortcrust and allowing them to cook inside the pastry.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked pasties on a tray. Bake from frozen at 180°C fan for 50 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch and freeze half unbaked.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble and refrigerate up to 12 hours before baking.

content.text: Cheese and onion pasty follows the same logic as a Cornish pasty: the filling goes in raw and cooks inside the pastry. The potato and onion need to be sliced thinly so they cook through in 45 minutes. The cheese must be strong: a mild cheddar will disappear into the filling and leave the pasty flat in flavour.

items.prepNote: peeled and very thinly sliced, about 2 mm

content.text: Mix together the sliced potato, sliced onion, and grated cheddar. Add the mustard powder if using. Season well with salt and pepper.

Divide the pastry into 4 equal pieces. Roll each into a circle about 25 cm across. Pile the filling onto one half of each circle, leaving a 2 cm border. Brush the border with beaten egg. Fold the pastry over, press the edges firmly together, and crimp along the top edge. Cut a small steam hole in the top.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Place the pasties on a lined baking tray. Brush with beaten egg. Bake for 20 minutes until set, then reduce to 180°C fan for a further 25 minutes until deeply golden. Rest for 5 minutes before eating.

items.symptom: The potato is still firm after baking
items.cause: The slices were too thick to cook through.
items.fix: Slice the potato as thinly as possible, 2 mm at most. A mandoline is useful here.

items.symptom: The cheese has run out of the pasty
items.cause: There was a gap in the crimp, or the seal was not pressed firmly.
items.fix: Press the edges together firmly before crimping. Any gap in the seal lets steam and melted cheese escape.

items.cause: The cheese was too mild or the filling underseasoned.
items.fix: Use a mature or extra-mature cheddar. Season the filling generously with salt and pepper before assembling.

items.symptom: The pastry is pale on the bottom
items.cause: The baking tray was too high in the oven, or the tray was not preheated.
items.fix: Bake on the middle or lower shelf of the oven. If the bottoms are consistently pale, try a darker metal tray.

content.text: Cheese and onion pasties are sold in every bakery in Britain and are a reliable lunchbox staple. They are easier to make than a Cornish pasty because there is no meat to worry about, and the strong cheese means the filling can carry the dish even without the complexity that beef fat brings. Eat them warm from the oven, or pack them cold; they travel well.
